summary: Build hundredths by subdividing a tenth again by ten, so children feel the recursive tenfold nesting: a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100), ten hundredths rebuild one tenth (10/100 = 1/10), and 100 hundredths make one whole. The central obstacle is whole-number bias — believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 > 10' — so comparing a single tenth against a single hundredth is a strongly recommended way to confront it. Derive hundredths by splitting a tenth, not by cutting the whole into 100 at once.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias on the denominator: believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 is bigger than 10'.
Not coordinating the nesting — treating 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as different, unrelated amounts.
Believing hundredths can only be made by cutting the whole into 100 at once, not by subdividing tenths (missing the recursive ×10 structure).
Losing count across the tenth boundary (after 9 hundredths, not seeing 10 hundredths = 1 tenth).
Thinking 'hundredths' refers to the large number 100 rather than to tiny parts of a whole.

activities.title: Split a tenth into ten hundredths
steps: Start with a strip that is one whole, already partitioned into ten equal tenths.
Take a single tenth and cut (or subdivide) it into ten equal pieces; name one piece 'a hundredth' and write 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100.

Work out how many of these small pieces would fill the whole strip: each of the ten tenths holds ten hundredths, so 10 × 10 = 100. Connect this to 'a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts of the whole'.
Count aloud in hundredths across the tenth boundary — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and pause at 10 hundredths to say it is also 1 tenth.
Lay one hundredth directly beside one tenth and describe how much smaller the hundredth is.
activities.insight: Hundredths come from dividing a tenth again by ten; ten hundredths rebuild one tenth and 100 hundredths make one whole. A hundredth is smaller than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10, because the same whole is split into more equal parts.

activities.title: Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary and place them on a line
steps: Count up and down in hundredths from 3/100 to 12/100, saying each amount aloud.
When the count reaches 10 hundredths, name the equivalent in tenths (10 hundredths = 1 tenth), and note that the pattern continues (20 hundredths = 2 tenths).
On a number line running from 0 to 1/10, mark the equal gaps needed to show hundredths and place 7/100 in the correct spot.
Explain how many equal gaps lie between 0 and 1 tenth and why.
activities.insight: Counting in hundredths and placing them between 0 and a tenth reinforces that each tenth holds exactly ten hundredths, so the count crosses cleanly into tenths.

activities.title: Predict and compare: which is bigger, a tenth or a hundredth?
steps: Before any cutting, predict which is bigger — one tenth or one hundredth — and state the reason.
Then split one tenth into ten and lay a single hundredth against a tenth.
Explain whether the result matches the prediction and why a hundredth is smaller despite 100 being larger than 10.
Answer: how many hundredths make one whole, and how do you know?
Consider: if one hundredth were split into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
activities.insight: A hundredth is smaller than a tenth; the whole-number intuition that '100 > 10 so a hundredth is bigger' is wrong because splitting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller. The ÷10 action repeats to make even smaller places.

checkQuestion: Start at 8 hundredths and count up in hundredths past ten: what comes after 9 hundredths, and what is another name for it? Then, if I take one tenth and split it into ten equal parts, what is each part called — and why?
checkAnswer: After 9 hundredths comes 10 hundredths, which is the same as 1 tenth; then 11, 12 hundredths. Splitting one tenth into ten gives hundredths (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100), because each place is a tenth of the one before; 100 hundredths make one whole.
